artworks.title: Cased Pocket Revolver, .28 Caliber, Massachusetts Arms Co., Massachusetts Arms Co., Chicopee Falls, MA
artworks.description:
This cased Massachusetts Arms Company pocket revolver is a .28 caliber six-shot pistol which has a 3″ octagonal barrel. This is a rare and important hand gun; rare because of its unusual and short-lived experimental ignition system, and important because it was made locally in the Connecticut River Valley.
The Massachusetts Arms Company was formed in 1849 by a group which included famous names in the gun business: Horace Smith, Daniel Wesson, Joshua Stephens and J. T. Ames. The Company, which was later incorporated in March of 1850, made many different kinds of firearms, including this cased set comprised of a pocket revolver, powder flask, bullet mold, nipple wrench and rammer. The .28 caliber pistol has a Maynard tape primer. This improvement in firearms was the invention of Edward Maynard who achieved his Patent in September of 1845. Instead of individual percussion caps, it depended upon a continuous roll of primer caps, not unlike a roll of child’s paper caps, which were advanced by a steel finger or a star wheel, positioning the cap atop a nipple where the hammer’s strike would ignite the fulminate and the charge in the chamber of the cylinder.
The grips are walnut. Originally finished blue, only vestiges of blueing survive on the trigger guard and barrel latch. Cylinder, frame, and cover plate are engraved with floral motifs. The top of frame is marked: “Mass. Arms Co. / Chicopee Falls”. Cover plate on side is marked: “Maynard’s Patent / Sept. 22, 1845”.

artworks.title: John Brown, Abraham Lincoln and the Civil War
artworks.description: Discover the Springfield story of John Brown, the passionate abolitionist whose years in the city helped shape his commitment to ending slavery and set the stage for one of the most dramatic events in American history. This exhibition explores Brown’s life in Springfield, his role in the abolitionist movement, and his infamous 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry. Through historic artifacts and personal belongings, visitors gain insight into the man behind the movement—including the challenges, convictions, and choices that defined his legacy. Highlights include Brown’s desk, where he helped hide freedom seekers as part of the Underground Railroad; wood and slate from his fort at Harpers Ferry; the hobnail safe from his Springfield wool business; his rocking chair, clay tobacco pipe, surveyor’s rule, and documents bearing his signature. The exhibition also shares the history of the Free Church of Springfield, an important center of abolitionist activity that was later renamed St. John’s Congregational Church in honor of John Brown. Together, these stories reveal Springfield’s important role in the national struggle over slavery and the pursuit of freedom. Sponsored by Mass Humanities, a state-based affiliate of the National Endowment for the Humanities, and Hampden Savings Foundation, Inc., the charitable foundation of Hampden Bank.

artworks.title: Uniform, Civil War Union Officer
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Mr. and. Mrs. Richard Knight, Jr.
artworks.description:
Edwin L. Knight was born in Brimfield on January 25, 1839. He was mustered into the United States Service, June 21 1861 as First Sergeant of Company E of the Massachusetts 10th. His promotions included Second Lieutenant July 21, 1862, Company G; Captain, January 1, 1863, Company E. He was severely wounded on his left side during the Battle of Spottslvania,VA on May 12, 1864. After serving his full three years of service, he was mustered out on July 21, 1864 as Brevet Major and returned to Springfield to work first for his father’s plumbing business and later at Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance Company.
Edwin L. Knight’s uniform is comprised of: a jacket; trousers; sash; leather belt; leather boots; and a leather cap box.

artworks.title: Granville Brothers Aircraft
artworks.description: Soar into Springfield’s aviation history and discover the daring innovation of the Granville Brothers Aircraft in this exhibition celebrating the golden age of air racing. In the late 1920s and early 1930s, brothers Zantford Granville and his siblings Edward, Robert, Thomas, and Mark built some of the fastest airplanes in the world right here in Springfield. Known as the “Gee Bee” aircraft, their sleek and powerful racing planes captured the imagination of pilots and aviation enthusiasts during a thrilling era of flight. See the only Zeta aircraft ever built, along with a three-quarter-scale replica of the legendary Gee Bee Model R-1, the racing plane flown by Jimmy Doolittle to victory in the 1932 Thompson Trophy race. The exhibit also features historic trophies, aviation artifacts, photographs, pilot memorabilia, and stories of aviation pioneers including Lowell Bayles, Jimmy Doolittle, Russell Boardman, and Maude Tait. Experience the innovation, ambition, and adventure that made the Granville Brothers—and their remarkable airplanes—a lasting part of Springfield’s place in aviation history.

artworks.description: This bicycle was used by George Hendee in his last year of championship racing competition. Hendee (1866–1943) was the leading American bicycle racer of the 1880s, winning 302 of 309 races entered. After he retired from racing he started his own bicycle manufacturing company in Springfield. His business acumen and leadership skills led to the founding of Indian Motocycle in 1901 as an outgrowth of his bicycle business.

artworks.title: The Esta Manthos Indian Motocycle Collection
artworks.description: Experience the story of one of America’s most iconic motorcycle brands in the Indian Motocycle Collection, home to the largest collection of Indian Motocycles and memorabilia in the world. Founded in Springfield in 1901, Indian Motocycle became a symbol of innovation, speed, and adventure. This remarkable collection showcases more than two dozen historic motocycles alongside photographs, artifacts, and memorabilia that trace the company’s rise from a local startup to a globally recognized manufacturer. See some of the rarest and most significant Indian Motocycles ever built, including a 1904 model personally designed and owned by co-founder Carl Oscar Hedstrom, a 1912 board track racing motocycle with its original racing tires, a beautifully restored 1929 101 Scout, and a rugged 1927 hill-climber. Along the way, discover the stories of the riders, racers, inventors, and workers who helped make Indian Motocycle a Springfield legend. From the company’s early days at the famous “Wigwam” factory to its contributions during times of war and its lasting influence on American motoring culture, this exhibition offers an unforgettable journey through more than half a century of ingenuity, craftsmanship, and Springfield history. artworks.title: Indian Scout 101, 1929, Indian Motocycle Co., Springfield, MA
artworks.description: Responding to feedback from racers, the original Indian Scout introduced in 1920 was updated with key modifications, making the new Scout 101 one of the most popular models ever built. Charles Franklin tweaked his original design, creating a bike that for years was a favorite among racers even though actual production years were few due to the onset of the Depression. The Scout 101 had a stronger frame, larger wheelbase, an increased fork rake, a front brake and a low 26¼ inch seat height. George Yarocki, local Indian collector and restorer, and former owner of this Scout 101 states “It’s a beautiful combination of weight and design … it handles like no other Indian motorcycle before or since.”

artworks.title: 1928 Indian Motocycle Company Roadster, X4, Indian Motocycle Co., Springfield, MA
artworks.description:
Indian Motocycle Company made four experimental cars, designated X1 through X4, between 1927 and 1928. This car is the fourth, X4. Featuring a roadster style body, this auto employed a Lycoming engine, WS 4037, and was used as a developmental car. It was designed by Assistant Project Engineer Harold F. Peavey, who had worked for Stevens-Duryea Automobile Company prior to his appointment at Indian Motocycle Company.
At the time these cars were developed Indian was experiencing difficult financial times. This led the Company to explore the possibility of introducing new products. Introducing an automobile seemed like a natural direction for Indian. Other projects included research on a two-cycle motocycle for the export market, and a 50 horsepower 45 cubic inch racing bike. They also developed a single unit refrigerator that never made it to market.
The experimental car project would, the company hoped, develop an auto that was a high performance commuter vehicle, easy to drive, easy to park, and with a comfortable ride. But when Charles Levine gained control of Indian late in 1929, just after the stock market crash, the enterprise was abandoned. Indian invested approximately $65,000 on the project, a significant blow to the company’s finances.
